name: Cloud Hypervisor
vendor: Cloud Hypervisor project (Linux Foundation), started at Intel
summary: A Rust virtual machine monitor for modern cloud VMs on KVM or Microsoft’s hypervisor: virtio devices only, plus hotplug, VFIO passthrough, live migration, snapshots and Windows guests.
intro: Cloud Hypervisor is a virtual machine monitor (VMM): the user-space program that creates a VM, emulates its devices and runs its vCPUs on a kernel hypervisor. It runs on Linux’s KVM or on the Microsoft Hypervisor (MSHV), the hypervisor underneath Hyper-V, where Linux runs as the root partition. It targets the VMs a cloud provider rents out: 64-bit guests whose I/O goes through paravirtualized virtio devices, with no need for legacy PC hardware. The device model is a handful of platform devices (a serial port, an RTC, an I/O APIC, ACPI shutdown and reboot) plus virtio block, network, console, IOMMU, persistent memory, RNG and vsock devices on a virtio-pci transport, and vhost-user devices that offload disk, network or filesystem work to another process. It boots a kernel directly (a PVH `vmlinux` or a `bzImage`) or a firmware: Rust Hypervisor Firmware, or an edk2 UEFI build that Windows guests need. It is written in Rust from the rust-vmm crates it shares with Firecracker and crosvm, and much of its code started in those two projects.

Unlike Firecracker, which is cut down for serverless functions, Cloud Hypervisor aims to be a general-purpose VMM. Each process runs one VM and is driven by its command line or a REST API (OpenAPI 3.0) on a Unix socket, which the bundled `ch-remote` tool calls. Through that API you can add vCPUs (x86 only) and memory to a running guest, hot-plug virtio disks, network cards, filesystems and vsock devices, pass host PCI devices through with VFIO, pause, snapshot and restore a VM, and live-migrate it over TCP, or over a Unix socket on the same host to upgrade the VMM with little downtime. Windows 10, Windows 11 and Windows Server guests run under KVM from UEFI images with virtio drivers. x86-64 and AArch64 (with a GICv3 interrupt controller) are the main architectures, and riscv64 is experimental.

Intel started the project in 2019 and it moved to the Linux Foundation in December 2021, backed by Alibaba, Arm, ByteDance, Intel and Microsoft. Kata Containers offers it as one of its VMMs, and Azure Kubernetes Service builds Pod Sandboxing from Kata Containers, Cloud Hypervisor and the Hyper-V hypervisor on Azure Linux hosts. Versions are numbered by major release, aiming for one about every six weeks; in practice they have come about every two months (v46.0 in May 2025 to v53.0 in July 2026). Each major release gets bug fixes for two cycles, about 12 weeks, and then reaches end of life.
strengths: A small, modern codebase: memory-safe Rust, a minimal virtio-based device model and no legacy devices, with the CLI, REST API and guest-visible devices covered by a stability policy (two major releases’ notice before breaking changes)
The lifecycle features general-purpose cloud VMs need: CPU, memory and device hotplug, VFIO passthrough, snapshot and restore, and live migration, including same-host migration for VMM upgrades
Runs Windows as well as Linux guests, on two hypervisors: KVM, or MSHV under a Linux root partition
Multi-vendor and in production use: a Linux Foundation project, a VMM option in Kata Containers, and part of AKS Pod Sandboxing
limits: A short support window: each major release gets fixes for about 12 weeks, and snapshots and live migration don’t work across major versions, so upgrades need planning
A building block, not a platform: you bring the kernel or firmware, disk images, tap devices and orchestration, or use a layer such as Kata Containers
Modern guests only: 64-bit, virtio drivers required, Windows only from UEFI images, CPU hotplug on x86 only, and live migration needs shared memory or huge pages

Advanced hardware support is thinner than QEMU’s: TDX, vfio-user and vDPA are experimental, and Kata’s docs list no GPU, TDX or SEV-SNP support for its Cloud Hypervisor runtime and point to QEMU for those

story: Intel started Cloud Hypervisor in 2019. Arjan van de Ven, an Intel Fellow and the project’s founding technical sponsor, later said the aim was “a more secure and updated VMM to optimize for modern cloud workloads”, with fewer device models and a memory-safe language. Instead of starting from nothing, the team built on the rust-vmm crates and on code from Firecracker and crosvm, the Rust VMMs from AWS and Google. Version 0.1.0 came out in July 2019 from Intel’s GitHub organization, already with VFIO device assignment, virtio-fs file sharing, virtio-pmem and direct boot of distribution `bzImage` kernels.

Where Firecracker trimmed a VMM down for short-lived serverless functions, Cloud Hypervisor aimed at the full range of cloud VMs. Version 0.10.0 (September 2020) added Windows guests. Microsoft, which since 2020 has been publishing open-source pieces for running Linux as the root partition of its own hypervisor, became one of the backers, and Cloud Hypervisor gained MSHV as a second backend next to KVM. On December 8, 2021 the project moved to the Linux Foundation, supported by Alibaba, Arm, ByteDance, Intel and Microsoft.

Today Kata Containers ships a Cloud Hypervisor configuration, and Azure Kubernetes Service uses it with Kata and the Hyper-V hypervisor for Pod Sandboxing. The project keeps a fast cadence of numbered major releases, reaching v53.0 in July 2026.

choices.choice: Build on rust-vmm instead of from scratch
choices.why: Rust’s memory and thread safety suit a security boundary, and importing shared crates (and code from Firecracker and crosvm) let three VMMs share components rather than each reimplementing KVM wrappers, memory handling and virtio devices.

choices.choice: Only modern cloud guests: 64-bit, virtio, no legacy devices
choices.why: Cloud customers run modern operating systems whose I/O already goes through paravirtualized devices. Dropping old PC hardware keeps emulation, attack surface, memory footprint and latency low.

The README sets it apart from Firecracker and crosvm by aiming at cloud workloads in general, not just containers, serverless or client devices. That is why it carries CPU, memory and PCI hotplug, VFIO, live migration and Windows support.
Running on MSHV as well as KVM lets the same VMM serve Linux hosts and hosts where Linux is the root partition of Microsoft’s hypervisor, as in AKS Pod Sandboxing.

timeline.text: Intel releases v0.1.0 in July, with VFIO, virtio-fs and virtio-pmem
Microsoft begins releasing components for Linux as root partition on its hypervisor; v0.10.0 adds Windows guests (September)
Moves to the Linux Foundation (December 8), backed by Alibaba, Arm, ByteDance, Intel and Microsoft
Major releases v46 to v50 arrive roughly every two months
